prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Security advisories for affected dependencies (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "CVE ID" · longest unbreakable word 46px · one-line width 125px
  col 2: header "Package" · longest unbreakable word 162px · one-line width 162px
  col 3: header "Affected versions" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 335px
  col 4: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 5: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable word 220px · one-line width 3094px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Help readers identify security advisories affecting dependencies, assess their severity, and understand the affected version ranges and issues.","reading":"Readers will scan CVE IDs and packages to find relevant advisories, then compare version ranges and severity before reading summaries; wrapped summaries can provide height for other cells to wrap within the same row.","groups":["CVE ID and Package identify the advisory and affected dependency.","Affected versions and Severity describe exposure and urgency; Summary explains the issue. Deeper summary wrapping can absorb wrapping elsewhere in the same row."],"keep_intact":["CVE IDs and package names should remain recognizable, especially long package paths.","Version numbers and comparison operators should stay together where possible.","Severity labels should remain on one line.","Long unbreakable terms in summaries need sufficient width or may be forced to break."],"may_wrap":["Affected version ranges can wrap between range clauses.","Summary prose can wrap naturally.","Headers can wrap where needed."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r2A: widths [146, 162, 90, 80, 241] · table 720×2115px · row heights [60, 385, 339, 315, 315, 362, 339] · column headers wrapped 1/5 · tallest cell 16 lines · mid-word splits 1
Design r2B: widths [146, 183, 84, 65, 241] · table 720×2115px · row heights [60, 385, 339, 315, 315, 362, 339] · column headers wrapped 2/5 · tallest cell 16 lines · mid-word splits 2
Design r2C: widths [146, 140, 112, 80, 241] · table 720×2115px · row heights [60, 385, 339, 315, 315, 362, 339] · column headers wrapped 1/5 · tallest cell 16 lines · mid-word splits 1

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
